tests.description: Positive value boundary: one Pod requests exactly the node's 500 millicore free CPU budget, so equality is feasible.
Positive existence boundary: node n2 has no selected target Pods, so its empty CPU sum is zero and fits a zero budget; p1 exactly fits n1.
Positive cardinality boundary: two assigned Pods are counted once each and their 40 plus 60 millicore requests exactly equal the 100 millicore budget.
Negative value boundary: a 501 millicore request exceeds the node's 500 millicore budget by one.
Negative cardinality case: each 60 millicore Pod would fit alone, but their joint 120 millicore request exceeds the 100 millicore node budget.
Positive equality boundary: one Pod requests exactly the node's available memory budget.
Positive zero boundary on an unused node: the assigned Pod fits n1, while n2 has zero selected requests and zero free memory.
Negative value boundary: the selected Pod exceeds free memory by one byte.
Negative shared-budget cardinality case: each Pod fits individually, but their combined selected requests exceed the node budget.
Positive value boundary: one target Pod exactly consumes the free units of one GPU resource.
Negative value boundary: the assigned Pod requests one unit more than the free GPU budget.
Inactive guard: a resource not identified as a GPU resource imposes no R3 budget constraint, even when its request exceeds its free value.
Positive cardinality boundary: two assigned Pods have requests that sum exactly to the node's GPU budget.
Negative cardinality boundary: each request fits individually, but the sum for two Pods exceeds the shared node-resource budget.
Distinct resource names are independent: surplus capacity for gpuB cannot satisfy a deficit for gpuA.
Equality boundary: two target Pods are assigned to the only node, which has exactly two remaining Pod slots.
Slack and zero-slot boundaries: the Pod uses one of two slots on n1, while the unused node n2 has zero slots and receives no target Pods.
Cardinality violation by one: two target Pods are assigned to a node with only one remaining Pod slot.
Zero-capacity violation: the only target Pod is assigned to the only node, whose remaining Pod-slot count is zero.
Positive singleton boundary: a scheduler-managed Pod assigned to the only node satisfies scheduling_tolerates.
Negative value boundary: a scheduler-managed Pod is assigned to a node where scheduling_tolerates is false.
Inactive scheduler guard: a direct nodeName Pod may be assigned even when scheduling_tolerates is false.
Negative multi-node cardinality boundary: toleration on an unassigned node cannot compensate for failure on the selected node.
Positive multi-node boundary: only the assigned node must satisfy scheduling_tolerates; an unassigned node may fail it.
A scheduler-managed Pod is assigned to one of two candidate nodes. Both requirements hold on the assigned node, while failures on the unassigned node are irrelevant.
The assigned scheduler-managed Pod fails its node selector even though required node affinity succeeds.
The assigned scheduler-managed Pod satisfies its node selector but fails required node affinity.
A Pod not using the scheduler is outside both guarded obligations, so false selector and affinity observations do not make the scenario infeasible.
Positive value boundary: one scheduler-managed Pod has exactly one candidate node, and required Pod affinity holds there.
Negative value boundary: the scheduler-managed Pod is assigned to its sole node, but required Pod affinity is false there.
Inactive-guard boundary: a Pod not using the scheduler may be assigned while pod_affinity_ok is false, because this category's scheduler guard is inactive.
Negative existence boundary: assignment choices remain free, but neither of two existing nodes satisfies required Pod affinity for the scheduler-managed Pod.
Positive cardinality boundary: two scheduler-managed target Pods are assigned to the sole node and each independently satisfies required Pod affinity at its scheduling step.
Positive value boundary: one scheduler-managed Pod is assigned to the sole node, where required Pod anti-affinity is satisfied.
Negative value boundary: the scheduler-managed Pod is assigned to a node where required Pod anti-affinity is false.
Inactive-guard case: a Pod not using the scheduler may be assigned by the shared model even when pod_anti_affinity_ok is false; this category imposes no consequence.
Assignment-guard boundary with two nodes: anti-affinity must hold on the assigned node, while failure on the unassigned node is irrelevant.

Cardinality and placement-existence boundary: with two candidate nodes and anti-affinity false on both, the shared exactly-one-assignment axiom leaves no valid assignment for the scheduler-managed Pod.
Positive topology-key boundary: one applicable hard spread constraint exists and the assigned node has its topology key; the separate skew obligation also remains valid.
Negative topology-key case: the hard spread constraint applies to a scheduler-managed assigned Pod, but the selected node lacks the required topology key.
Inactive scheduler guard: because the Pod is not scheduler-managed, a missing topology key does not activate the topology-key obligation.
Positive skew equality boundary: prior count 1 plus self-match 1 minus global minimum 1 equals maxSkew 1.
Negative skew boundary: prior count 1 plus self-match 1 minus global minimum 0 is 2, exceeding maxSkew 1 by one.
Inactive applicability guard: the arithmetic would exceed maxSkew, but the hard spread constraint does not apply to this Pod, so no skew obligation is imposed.
Existence boundary: with no hard Spread objects, both universally quantified obligations are vacuous and the assignment remains feasible for this category.
Cardinality boundary with two applicable hard constraints: the first satisfies its skew limit, while the second exceeds its limit, demonstrating that every hard constraint is checked.
A single referenced PVC exists and its fixed-volume reference is valid, satisfying both obligations at the one-reference boundary.
The Pod references a PVC that does not exist. The claim-existence obligation fails while the fixed-reference guard remains inactive.
The referenced PVC exists, but its explicitly named or already bound PV does not exist, violating the fixed-reference obligation.
No target Pod references the claim, so a false claim-existence value imposes no S1 claim obligation.
The claim exists but is not referenced by the target Pod, so a false fixed-volume-existence value imposes no fixed-reference obligation.
At the multiple-reference boundary, one valid referenced claim does not compensate for a second referenced claim that is missing.
A single existing referenced PVC selecting dynamic provisioning is feasible at the positive boundary when the class, provisioner, and parameters are all valid.
An existing referenced PVC selecting dynamic provisioning is infeasible when its effective StorageClass does not exist, while the other configuration obligations hold.
An existing referenced PVC selecting dynamic provisioning is infeasible when no valid provisioner is configured, while the class and parameter obligations hold.
An existing referenced PVC selecting dynamic provisioning is infeasible when its provisioner parameters do not pass the matching validation contract, while the class and provisioner obligations hold.
When static rather than dynamic provisioning is selected, invalid dynamic configuration observations impose no S2 obligation.
At the PVC existence boundary, a referenced identity not known to exist does not activate the dynamic configuration obligations.
A dynamic PVC not referenced by the target Pod does not activate this category's configuration obligations.
At a larger finite cardinality boundary, two Pods may reference two dynamically provisioned PVCs when every existing referenced claim satisfies all three configuration obligations.
At the zero-Volume cardinality boundary, an existing referenced claim is satisfiable through selected dynamic provisioning when it is dynamically eligible.
At the zero-Volume cardinality boundary, a guarded claim is unsatisfiable when dynamic provisioning is unselected because no static or dynamic path remains.
Two target Pods may share one fixed PVC whose selected PV passes every static compatibility check and is the designated fixed volume.
A selected static PV is rejected when its storage class is incompatible, while every other static compatibility conjunct holds.
A selected static PV is rejected when it does not provide all requested access modes, while every other compatibility conjunct holds.
A selected static PV is rejected when its volume mode differs from the claim mode, while every other compatibility conjunct holds.
